title: How Spiders Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore spiders: their diversity (about 40,000 known species), how they differ from insects (arachnids with a cephalothorax and abdomen, eight legs, pedipalps), breathing via tracheae and book lungs, hemolymph circulation, tiny nervous systems and jumping spider vision, senses based on vibration and trichobothria, molting and hydraulic leg movement, spider silk strength and the goat-milk silk project, web building (orb webs), hunting methods, venom and dangerous spiders (brown recluse, Sydney funnel-web, Brazilian wandering spider), spider mating, and the diving bell spider. The episode closes with listener mail about a dog donating blood to another dog.

segments.title: Opening banter and spider basics
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about spiders being everywhere, the Baltimore wastewater plant infestation, and how spiders are arachnids, not insects, with a cephalothorax, abdomen, and eight legs plus pedipalps.

segments.title: Body, breathing, and circulation
segments.summary: Discussion of spider body layout, breathing through tracheae and book lungs, and hemolymph pumped through the body instead of closed blood vessels.

segments.title: Spider brains, vision, and senses
segments.summary: Spiders have ganglia rather than true brains; jumping spiders have around 100,000 neurons yet good vision with eight eyes. Spiders sense vibrations through leg hairs and trichobothria, and can taste.

segments.title: Molting and hydraulic leg movement
segments.summary: Spiders move legs by hydraulic pressure from hemolymph rather than muscles extending them, can dehydrate with curled legs, and molt their exoskeleton, growing in a vulnerable soft period.

segments.title: Spider silk and the goat-milk project
segments.summary: Spider silk is a liquid extruded from spinnerets that hardens when stretched; it is very strong, stronger than steel and Kevlar by weight, and comparable to rubber in flexibility. Researchers engineered goats to produce drag line silk proteins in their milk, with potential uses like ligaments and hearts. Silk uses include drag lines, sticky threads, water-resistant coatings, cocoons, and net casting.

segments.title: Building an orb web
segments.summary: The hosts walk through how an orb-weaving spider builds its web: a bridge line, a lazy V, frame threads, a spiral of sticky silk laid while eating the temporary spiral, and waiting at the center for vibrations. Spiders also recycle old webs by eating them.

segments.title: Hunting methods, venom, and dangerous spiders
segments.summary: Spiders hunt by trapdoor ambush, stalking (wolf and jumping spiders), and webs. Venom is usually neurotoxic and digestion is external. Brown recluse, Sydney funnel-web, and Brazilian wandering spider are discussed, with the brown recluse noted for necrosis and the funnel-web anti-venom developed around 1980. Daddy longlegs (harvestmen) are discussed as harmless and lacking venom.

segments.title: Spider mating and the diving bell spider
segments.summary: Male spiders seek females, may court with dances or plucked web vibrations, deposit sperm via pedipalps, and risk being eaten. Females lay many eggs and may guard them. Tarantula fear discussion and the diving bell spider, which builds an air bubble underwater, close the topic.

segments.title: Listener mail: dog blood donation
segments.summary: A listener named Kara from Lexington, Kentucky describes her fifty-six-pound dog Hatchet donating blood to another dog in an emergency.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts plug website, social media, and email contact information.
